doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Arbors session routine: two four-hour days
summary: Sessions are booked for two four-hour days, often with no advance material; leading sessions with players like Warren Vache and Harry Allen.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How much time do you get — like you’re on a lot of the Arbors recordings now, and how much time do you typically get. This is a long question. But how many hours do those LPs — yeah LPs — do those CDs actually take, and do you know what’s coming before you get there?

Uh good question. Okay assuming I’m not the leader I have no clue what’s coming until I get there. So the session usually is booked for two four hour days, 12 to 4 on a Monday, 12 to 4 on a Tuesday. They’re usually consecutive days. And so you turn up at 12 and you might get a bunch of tunes in your hand. You might get a tune for a song. You know what I mean? Like we’re doing this song, here’s the music. Do that song. Here’s the next

song. Here’s — either you know it or they’ll give you a chart you know what I mean? If they’ve got a specific arrangement they’ll always pull a chart. And so if I’m not the leader I have no clue what we’re doing. If I’m the leader and I think the musicians don’t need to know until they get there, you know what I mean, like when you’re playing with such wonderful players like Warren Vache and Harry Allen, they can read and play through anything. You don’t really have to worry about it, you just turn up and you get to rehearse it. If it’s hard you rehearse it. But then if I’m leading myself and I want to sing some then you do two days of instrumental and then usually I come in on another day and finish up the vocals or something.
